items.headline: The central claim the whole literature chase existed to support: σ ≈ 0.6 is approximately one unit of real experimental measurement error for the paper's endpoints.
items.verbatim: **The idea.** The paper sweeps $\sigma$ from 0 to 1 and never says what those numbers mean physically. A reviewer can reasonably ask "why 0.5? why 1.0? is any of this the amount of noise real data actually has?" There is a published answer, and it is a strong one: **for the endpoints in this paper, $\sigma \approx 0.6$ is approximately one unit of real experimental measurement error.** That converts an arbitrary knob into a claim worth making.
items.why_it_matters: This is the single sentence the whole 31-agent literature search was run to license. Without it σ is an arbitrary knob and a reviewer can dismiss the entire sweep.

items.headline: The units argument that makes the comparison legitimate — noise is injected in raw label units and all three external labels are logs.
items.verbatim: **Why the comparison is legitimate — the units line up.** Noise is injected as $y_\text{noisy} = y + \sigma \cdot \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ in the label's own **raw units** (`NoiseInject/noiseInject/core.py:68`; only $X$ is standardised, never $y$). And all three external labels are on a log scale: logD natively, hERG as $pK_i$, and Caco-2 efflux via `log_transform=True` at `KIRBy/tests/alternative_data_noise_robustness.py:1256`. So $\sigma$ is directly comparable to a published assay error quoted in log units — no conversion, no hand-waving.
items.why_it_matters: Without this the σ↔assay-error comparison is a category error. It also names the exact two code lines that ground it, so it can be re-checked.

items.headline: The scale-free conclusion drawn from the table: assay error in log units is roughly constant across endpoints regardless of label spread.
items.verbatim: Every estimate falls roughly between 0.4 and 0.74, clustered near 0.5–0.6 — **regardless of endpoint**. That is the useful fact: assay error in log units is roughly scale-free across these assays. (The range was previously written as "0.27–0.74" on the strength of the Bruneau figure; with that number withdrawn, the verified logD support is Niu 2024's MAE 0.48, which sits comfortably inside the same band and does not change the conclusion.)
items.why_it_matters: This is the argument that kills per-dataset label-SD matching and licenses a single fixed σ. It also records that withdrawing Bruneau did NOT change the conclusion.

items.headline: The paste-ready Methods sentence anchoring σ to published assay error (drafted, pending insertion).
items.verbatim:
**Draft sentence for Methods (pending the D11 decision — do not insert yet):**
> Noise magnitudes are reported in the units of the label itself. Because all external endpoints are expressed on a logarithmic scale, the injected $\sigma$ is directly comparable to published estimates of experimental measurement error, which lie between roughly 0.4 and 0.7 log units for $pK_i$ [Kramer 2012], $pIC_{50}$ [Kalliokoski 2013], logD [Niu 2024] and hERG potency under standardised protocols [Alvarez Baron 2025]. An injected $\sigma$ of 0.6 therefore corresponds to approximately one additional unit of the measurement error already present in public bioactivity data.

*(Citation set updated after verification: Bruneau 2006 and Hayeshi 2008 are dropped from the draft sentence — neither number survived checking. Kalliokoski, Niu and Alvarez Baron are all open access and fully verified.)*
items.why_it_matters: This is finished prose the author can paste. Losing it means re-drafting from scratch, and the post-verification citation swap (drop Bruneau and Hayeshi) would be silently undone.

items.headline: Four caveats that must travel with the σ=0.6 claim — QM9 exclusion, quadrature doubling, weak Caco-2 evidence, intra- vs inter-lab.
items.verbatim:
1. **QM9 is computed data.** Its labels come from DFT, so there is no experimental error to match and this justification does not transfer. $\sigma$ on QM9 is a controlled perturbation, not a simulation of measurement noise, and the paper must say so rather than letting the reader carry the ADME framing across.
2. **The error is already in the data.** Public labels *already* carry this noise; injecting $\sigma = 0.6$ roughly doubles it rather than creating it. Errors add in quadrature: $\sqrt{0.54^2 + 0.6^2} \approx 0.81$. Phrase it as "an additional unit", never as "we introduce realistic noise into clean data".
3. **The Caco-2 evidence is the weakest of the three.** ... **Cite the underlying Hayeshi 10-lab study instead**, where atenolol alone spans 0.18 to 3.76 across laboratories.
items.why_it_matters: Each caveat pre-empts a specific referee objection. Caveat 2 in particular changes the required wording from 'we add realistic noise' to 'an additional unit'.

items.headline: Caveat 4 — intra-lab and inter-lab figures must not be swapped, and Alvarez Baron's τ=0.18 is a within-lab residual.
items.verbatim: 4. **Intra- vs inter-laboratory matters and is easy to misquote.** The 0.17–0.22 $pIC_{50}$ figures are a single-lab repeatability floor; the 0.54–0.68 figures are inter-laboratory. Public databases aggregate many sources, so the inter-laboratory number is the relevant one. Alvarez Baron et al. 2025 (*Sci. Rep.* **15**:29995) report $\tau = 0.18$, which despite being a five-lab study is a *within*-lab residual — do not quote it as an inter-lab error.
items.why_it_matters: τ=0.18 looks like an inter-lab number and is not. Quoting it that way would make the injected σ look 3× too large relative to reality.

items.headline: The abandoned approach, recorded with its reason: matching σ to each dataset's label spread is the wrong normaliser.
items.verbatim: **This also corrects an approach I proposed and then abandoned.** I had suggested matching $\sigma$ to each dataset's label spread, so that noise was a constant fraction of signal. That is the wrong normaliser: assay error in log units is roughly constant across endpoints *irrespective* of how spread out the labels are, so a fixed $\sigma$ in log units is more defensible than a per-dataset one. The label-spread ratios remain useful for one narrow purpose — explaining why Caco-2 degrades earliest, since its labels are the most tightly spread (SD 0.434 against 1.19 for logD, so a given $\sigma$ is ~2.7$\times$ harsher there).
items.why_it_matters: Records a whole abandoned design branch and the one purpose the label-SD ratios survive for. Without it the SD-matching idea would be re-proposed.

items.headline: Kramer 2012 — the pKi headline numbers, verbatim from the abstract: SD 0.54, mean error 0.44, median error 0.34.
items.verbatim:
> "The experimental uncertainty is estimated to yield a mean error of 0.44 pK(i) units, a standard deviation of 0.54 pK(i) units, and a median error of 0.34 pK(i) units."

*Location: abstract.*
Gives a directly citable magnitude — σ ≈ 0.54 in log units for heterogeneous public binding-affinity data — so a noise-injection sweep spanning roughly σ = 0.1 to 0.5 can be described as running from optimistic to realistic rather than as an arbitrary range.
items.verification: verified (independently re-fetched and re-checked character-for-character; abstract only — full text never retrieved)
items.why_it_matters: The hERG anchor. 0.54 is the number the paper's σ=0.6 is compared against, and this is the exact quotable sentence.

items.headline: Kramer 2012 — rendering note: 'pK(i)' is the MEDLINE ASCII convention; the ACS PDF prints pKᵢ.
items.verbatim: *Note on rendering:* "pK(i)" is the MEDLINE ASCII de-subscripting convention. The ACS-published version prints pKᵢ with a subscript, so a transcription from the publisher PDF would read "0.54 pKi units".
items.why_it_matters: Prevents a referee or co-author flagging the quote as a mis-transcription when checked against the publisher PDF.

items.headline: Kramer 2012 — the reproducibility-definition sentence: what is being measured is the spread between independent repeat measurements.
items.verbatim:
> "The data deposited in ChEMBL was analyzed for reproducibility, i.e., the experimental uncertainty of independent measurements."

*Location: abstract, fifth sentence.*
Establishes that the quantity being measured is the spread between genuinely independent repeat measurements of the same quantity, which is exactly the quantity a σ-sized Gaussian perturbation of a log-unit label is meant to imitate.
items.why_it_matters: Establishes that Kramer's 0.54 measures the same physical quantity the injected Gaussian imitates — the justification for treating them as commensurable.

items.headline: Kramer 2012 — the curation-required sentence, plus the caveat that '90%' attaches only to repeated citations, not to pairs discarded.
items.verbatim:
> "Careful filtering of the data was required because ChEMBL contains unit-transcription errors, undifferentiated stereoisomers, and repeated citations of single measurements (90% of all pairs)."

*Caveat, important:* the abstract does **not** say 90% of pairs were removed. The parenthetical attaches to the third list item only — repeated citations of single measurements. Any gloss along the lines of "90% of pairs were discarded" goes beyond what the retrieved text supports, and the paywalled Methods would be needed to check it.
items.verification: verified (quote); the '90% of pairs discarded' gloss is explicitly NOT supported
items.why_it_matters: A very easy misquote to make. Also supports the honest statement that the 0.54 figure applies to curated, not raw, repository data.

items.headline: Kramer 2012 access status — abstract only, ACS returns HTTP 403; fetched via Europe PMC and cross-checked against PMID 22643060.
items.verbatim: **Access. ABSTRACT ONLY.** The ACS landing page (`https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/jm300131x`) returns HTTP 403. Abstract fetched from the Europe PMC REST API: `https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=DOI:%2210.1021/jm300131x%22&resultType=core&format=json`, and cross-checked against PubMed PMID 22643060. **No full text was retrieved for this paper.**
items.why_it_matters: Bounds exactly what can be quoted from Kramer: three numbers and two sentences, nothing else.

items.headline: Kramer 2012 — the R² = 0.81 ceiling on large datasets, with an attribution warning that it is not a universal ceiling.
items.verbatim:
**The ceiling this imposes**, verbatim from Kramer et al. 2012:

> "The maximum possible squared Pearson correlation coefficient (R²) on large data sets is
> estimated to be **0.81**."
> "Models that yield errors smaller than the experimental uncertainty are necessarily
> overtrained."

⚠️ Attribute as *estimated for heterogeneous public Ki data with SD 0.54 pKi units*, not as
a universal ceiling — the derivation is in the paywalled body and is unverified.
items.verification: unverified (the derivation is in the paywalled body; the quote itself is presented as verbatim but the guide flags the claim's scope as unverified)
items.why_it_matters: The strongest available 'why does label noise matter at all' framing sentence for the paper's introduction — but only if attributed narrowly.

items.headline: Kalliokoski 2013 — the pIC50 headline: σ = 0.68, MUE 0.55, MedUE 0.43, with a caveat that the 0.55 is a scaled estimate.
items.verbatim:
> "For heterogeneous biochemical pIC50 data, we find a variability with σpIC50 = 0.68, MUEpIC50 = 0.55 and MedUEpIC50 = 0.43."

*Location: Summary and Conclusions; the same figures also appear in the Discussion.*

*Caveat:* the verification pass flagged that the 0.55 MUE in this sentence is an estimate obtained by scaling the pKi metrics upward by 25%; the paper's directly measured MUE from ΔpIC50 data with a 2.5 threshold is 0.54, not 0.55. That alternative sentence was not part of the independently confirmed set, so it is reported here as a caution only and must not be quoted from this document. The σ = 0.68 figure is unaffected.
items.verification: verified (σ=0.68); the MUE 0.55 carries a flagged caveat and must not be quoted from the guide
items.why_it_matters: 0.68 is the upper anchor of the range and the single best-evidenced number in the whole set. The MUE caveat prevents quoting a derived figure as a measured one.

items.headline: Kalliokoski 2013 — the fold-change translation of σ = 0.68: 68.2% of IC50 measurements agree within a factor of 4.8.
items.verbatim:
> "A standard deviation of 0.68 corresponds to a factor of 4.8, meaning that 68.2% of all IC50 measurements agree within a factor of 4.8, even when measured in different laboratories under potentially different assay conditions."

*Location: Discussion, second paragraph.*
Translates a log-unit σ into a concentration-fold interpretation, which lets a noise-injection paper explain to a non-modelling reader what σ = 0.68 physically means without inventing its own conversion.
items.why_it_matters: Lets the paper explain what a log-unit σ means to a chemist without doing its own arithmetic — a published conversion is far safer than an invented one.

items.headline: Kalliokoski 2013 — the intra-laboratory floor: σ = 0.22 (rolipram/PDE4D) and σ = 0.17 (cilostamide/PDE3).
items.verbatim:
> "IC50 values measured in the same laboratory usually show a better reproducibility. From our in-house database, we extracted series of reference pIC50 values measured for assay standards. The plots in Figure 9 show the pIC50 values measured for rolipram on PDE4D and cilostamide on PDE3. The standard deviation of the pIC50 values are σ = 0.22 for rolipram/PDE4D and σ = 0.17 for cilostamide/PDE3."

*Location: Discussion, the paragraph introducing Figure 9.*
Provides the low end of the realistic range — σ ≈ 0.17–0.22 for repeat measurements within one laboratory — so a σ sweep can be anchored at both ends with measured values rather than round numbers.
items.why_it_matters: Anchors the LOW end of the σ ladder with a measured number. Also the source of the λ=3 contamination ratio (0.68/0.17–0.22 = 3.1–4.0).

items.headline: Kalliokoski 2013 — the sample size behind σ=0.68: 20,356 independent measurement pairs, with a thousands-separator transcription warning.
items.verbatim:
> "From the initially available 616.555 IC50 values with confidence score greater or equal to four 10.895 IC50 values for 3.480 Protein/Ligand systems remained, yielding 20.356 pairs of independent measurements."

*Location: Materials and Methods → "Dataset Preparation", the paragraph immediately preceding Table 1.* (A verification pass corrected this from "Results"; the paper uses "." as a thousands separator, so this is 616,555 → 10,895 values, 3,480 systems, 20,356 pairs.)
items.verification: verified (with a location correction applied by the verification pass)
items.why_it_matters: Lets the paper present 0.68 as well-powered rather than anecdotal. The '.' thousands separator would otherwise be transcribed as a decimal point.

items.headline: Kalliokoski 2013 — the √2 correction: a σ from measurement PAIRS must be divided by √2 to get the per-measurement σ.
items.verbatim:
> "Note that since the σ here is calculated from pairs of measurements each containing experimental uncertainty and other sources of variability, it has to be divided by √2 in order to obtain the true σ of the individual measurements [13]."

*Location: Kalliokoski et al. 2013, caption of Figure 5.*
This is the single most important methodological point for a noise-injection paper: a σ computed from differences between duplicate measurements is √2 larger than the σ of one measurement, so the value injected into a label must be the per-measurement σ, not the pairwise one.
items.verification: verified — but this is Kalliokoski's sentence, NOT Kramer's; must be attributed to Kalliokoski 2013
items.why_it_matters: Called 'the single most important methodological point for a noise-injection paper'. Getting it wrong makes every quoted σ 41% too large.

items.headline: Kalliokoski 2013 — a re-analysis of Kramer's data lands at 0.47, not 0.54, so σ≈0.5 should be quoted as an approximate anchor.
items.verbatim:
> "After dividing by √2, the σ for the Gaussian distribution fitted to all ΔpKi values <2.5 then becomes 0.47 (a bit lower than the σ value of 0.54 previously calculated for heterogeneous pKi data from ChEMBL version 12 data without upper threshold for ΔpKi data."

*Location: Kalliokoski et al. 2013, Results/Discussion, the paragraph following Table 3.*
Shows that the 0.54 figure is sensitive to how outlying pairs are handled — a comparable re-analysis lands at 0.47 — which supports quoting σ ≈ 0.5 as an approximate anchor rather than a precise constant.

*Note:* the unbalanced open parenthesis is genuinely in the published text and has been reproduced rather than tidied.
items.verification: verified (including the unbalanced parenthesis, reproduced deliberately)
items.why_it_matters: Prevents over-claiming 0.54 as a precise constant. Also flags a typography trap: the unbalanced parenthesis will look like a transcription error.

items.headline: Kalliokoski 2013 — public aggregated data is noisier than single-laboratory data, which justifies sweeping σ rather than fixing one value.
items.verbatim:
> "The standard deviation of public ChEMBL IC50 data, as expected, resulted greater than the standard deviation of in-house intra-laboratory/inter-day IC50 data."

*Location: abstract.*
Establishes that label noise is not one number but a function of provenance — public aggregated data is noisier than single-laboratory data — which justifies sweeping σ rather than fixing a single value.
items.why_it_matters: The published justification for running a σ SWEEP at all, rather than a single calibrated level.

items.headline: Kalliokoski 2013 — measurement error does NOT depend on the value measured, tested directly on 16,844 repeat pairs.
items.verbatim:
> "We checked whether the ΔpIC50 depends on the overall activity measured or on
> physicochemical ligand properties like logP, logD, molecular weight (MW), polar surface
> area (PSA), the number hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), the number hydrogen bond donors
> (HBD) or the number of rotatable bonds... **The ΔpIC50's depend neither on the average
> measured pIC50 nor on any of the ligand properties examined.**"

> "One might assume that higher IC50 values show a larger variability than for example
> single digit µM IC50 values because of solubility limits. **However, our analysis shows
> that on the average this is clearly not the case.**"
items.why_it_matters: This is the empirical basis for DROPPING four of the six noise strategies (threshold, quantile, value-proportional, heteroscedastic) — they all assume error scales with the label value, and that premise is directly refuted here.

items.headline: Kalliokoski 2013 — real error is not Gaussian in the tail; the guide computes how wrong a Gaussian is at 2, 3 and 4 log units.
items.verbatim:
**Kalliokoski et al. (2013)** could only fit a Gaussian after truncating at 1.5–2.5 log
units, and the fitted width grows with the cut (0.80 → 0.84 → 0.86). The largest single
disagreement is **7.7 log units** — a nine-sigma event that a Gaussian says should occur
6×10⁻¹⁵ times in 16,844 pairs. It occurred once.

How wrong a Gaussian is in the tail *(computed from their Figure 2)*:

| Disagreement | Observed | Gaussian predicts | Wrong by |
|---|---|---|---|
| > 2 log units | 9.0% | 4.7% | 1.9× |
| > 3 log units | 2.2% | 0.29% | 7.7× |
| > 4 log units | 0.40% | 0.007% | **58×** |

Fitting the full tail gives Student-t with **ν ≈ 4–6**; fitting only the truncated core
gives ν ≈ 8–16.
items.verification: computed by the author from Kalliokoski's Figure 2 (marked as computed, not quoted)
items.why_it_matters: Quantifies exactly how badly a homoscedastic Gaussian misrepresents real error, and sets the ν parameter for the replacement Student-t noise type.

items.headline: Honest limitation: matching the real tail would need ν≈1.1, which has no finite variance and cannot be dose-matched.
items.verbatim:
⚠️ **Honest limitation to state in the paper:** matching the *real* tail needs about
ν = 1.1, which has no finite variance and therefore cannot be dose-matched. Strategy 2 at
ν = 3 is a **conservative** heavy-tailed setting. Real data is heavier than anything that can
be fairly tested.
items.why_it_matters: Pre-empts the obvious referee question 'why only ν=3?' and turns a limitation into a stated, defensible design choice.

items.headline: Kalliokoski 2013 Table 2 — the extreme tail of disagreement is database ERROR, not imprecision.
items.verbatim:
Kalliokoski's Table 2 manually inspected 10 pairs per disagreement band. Number invalid:
Δ 4.7–7.8 → **9/10**; Δ 3.2 → **10/10**; Δ 2.5 → **8/10**; Δ 1.5 → 6/10; Δ 1.1 → 1/10;
Δ 0.02 → 0/10. Error types named: unit-transcription, receptor-subtype confusion,
cellular-versus-biochemical assay mix-up, undifferentiated stereochemistry, retracted papers.

> "The extreme disagreements are all due to clear errors."

This is why strategy 5 is called Outlier and why its victims are chosen at random: a
mistyped unit is a property of the *record*, not of the value.
items.verification: verified (quote); the 9/10, 10/10, 8/10 breakdown is read from their Table 2
items.why_it_matters: This is the published justification for the Outlier noise type AND for changing its selection rule from 'extreme labels' to 'random records'.

items.headline: Sato 2018 — the measured agreement ceiling between two hERG assay technologies: R² = 0.517, RMSD = 0.737 log units on 209 compounds.
items.verbatim:
> "The coefficient of determination and the root mean square deviation between the pIC50 values measured by binding assays and electrostatic assays were 0.517 and 0.737, respectively."

*Location: Results and discussion → "Comparison between binding assays and electro static assays".*
Gives a measured ceiling on agreement between two experimental methods — R² = 0.517, RMSD = 0.737 log units — which is the most direct available justification for the claim that a model cannot be expected to beat a certain error floor on aggregated hERG labels.

*Caveat:* R² = 0.517 here is agreement between two assay technologies, **not** a predictive model's R². If this is used as a performance ceiling it must be framed as inter-assay-method agreement.
items.why_it_matters: 0.737 is the upper end of the assay-error band and the most direct 'why the model can't do better' number. The caveat prevents it being mistaken for a model R².

items.headline: Sato 2018 — the 209-compound cross-assay sample size.
items.verbatim:
> "To compare the two methods, 209 compounds for which the IC50 values were measured by both methods were investigated."

*Location: Results and discussion → "Comparison between binding assays and electro static assays".* (The two-word "electro static" is the published heading.)
items.why_it_matters: Gives the basis for the 0.737 figure. The 'electro static' two-word heading is a published typo that must be reproduced, not corrected.

items.headline: Sato 2018 — real hERG label error is heavy-tailed: of 263 compounds, 144 agree within one order of magnitude but 47 disagree by more than 100-fold.
items.verbatim:
> "Among the 263 compounds, 144 compounds showed consistent IC50 values with less than one order of magnitude differences between the maximum and minimum results. However, 47 compounds recorded more than 100-fold differences between the maximum and minimum IC50 values."

*Location: Results and discussion → "Deviation of IC50 values and classification of hERG inhibitors and inactive compounds" (the paragraph after Fig 4).*
Establishes that real label error is heavy-tailed — most compounds agree within one log unit but a substantial minority disagree by more than two — which is a concrete, citable limitation of a homoscedastic Gaussian noise model and a motivation for outlier-style or heteroscedastic noise strategies.
items.why_it_matters: A second, independent published demonstration of heavy tails — the citable motivation for the Outlier and Student-t noise types.

items.headline: Sato 2018 — hERG label noise is partly structural: two different assay technologies measuring different physical things.
items.verbatim:
> "The assay protocols of hERG blocking activities could roughly classified into electrostatic assays such as automated patch clamp assays that measure the change in the voltage between the cell-membrane by the presence of small molecules, and binding assays, such as radio-ligand replacement assays that measure the binding affinity of small molecules by the replacement ratio of radiolabeled inhibitors."

*Location: Materials and methods → "Formatting activity information".* (The missing "be" in "could roughly classified" is in the original.)
items.verification: verified (the grammatical error is in the original and is reproduced deliberately)
items.why_it_matters: Supports framing label noise as systematic-plus-random rather than purely random. The 'could roughly classified' error must be reproduced or the quote will look mis-transcribed.

items.headline: Sato 2018 — assay-protocol heterogeneity is treated in the literature as a first-class source of label deviation (location corrected to the Introduction).
items.verbatim:
> "Since the integrated dataset contained heterogeneous data entries, the deviations of the hERG inhibitory activities due to the differences in the assay protocols were analyzed, to assess the influence of the deviations on the classification of the tested compounds into hERG inhibitors and non-inhibitors."

*Location: **Introduction** — a verification pass corrected this from "Materials and methods → Data set". In the Introduction it reads as a stated aim of the study, not as an executed procedure, and should be cited that way.*
items.verification: verified, with a location correction applied by the verification pass
items.why_it_matters: Records a location correction that would be silently lost. Citing it as an executed procedure rather than a stated aim would be an over-claim.

items.headline: FAILED VERIFICATION — the Bruneau & McElroy 2006 'logD 0.27 log units across 307 compounds' figure has no verified quote and must not be used.
items.verbatim: **LogD from Bruneau & McElroy 2006: the "0.27 log units across 307 compounds" figure has no verified quote.** This is the significant gap. Three separate claimed sentences from this paper's Methodology and Results — the one containing 0.27 and 307, the preceding clause about the 2-log-unit exclusion threshold, and two sentences from the "Database" subsection including a 0.3-log-unit discard threshold — all failed verification with the verdict "could not access". The ACS full text returns HTTP 403, Unpaywall reports the article as closed with zero repository copies, and only the abstract could be read; the abstract contains none of those numbers.
items.why_it_matters: This is the single number in the whole set that would be a hallucination if published. It is currently cited in two repo files and must be struck from both.

items.headline: Bruneau 2006 — the three honest options for the 0.27 number, in order of preference.
items.verbatim:
1. **Obtain the PDF manually** through Oxford institutional access at pubs.acs.org, or from the archived author copy, and check pages 1380 and 1382–1383 by eye. This is the only route that turns 0.27 into a quotable figure, and it is cheap.
2. **Cite without quoting.** Write "Bruneau and McElroy report a mean per-compound replicate standard deviation of approximately 0.27 log units for in-house logD7.4 data" with a plain citation and no quotation marks. This is defensible only if you have actually seen the number somewhere you trust; do not do this on the strength of this document alone, because this document has not confirmed it.
3. **Use a different source.** PharmaBench Table 5 (MAE 0.48–0.7 for LogD) is fully verified, open access, and covers the same endpoint.
items.why_it_matters: Names the exact pages (1380, 1382–1383) to check by eye. This is the cheapest route to closing the only failed-verification gap in the set.

items.headline: Bruneau 2006 — the ONE quote that did survive verification: a selection-bias warning about replicate-derived error estimates.
items.verbatim:
> "A measurement is more likely repeated if an apparently abnormal result is obtained. Thus, high ranges in duplicated measurements do not indicate a global variability of the experimental methodology."

*Location: reference/endnote list, note (32), final page — the note cited at the point in the text where the replicate-variability estimate is given.*
Establishes a selection-bias warning that directly constrains any noise-injection justification: replicate spreads in industrial datasets are not a random sample of measurement error, because repeats are preferentially triggered by suspicious results, so replicate-derived σ estimates skew high.
items.verification: verified — retrieved from an author-hosted PDF via the Internet Archive (https://web.archive.org/web/20240423025829if_/https://www.people.iup.edu/nate/docs/ci0504014.pdf); other passes could not reach any full text
items.why_it_matters: A genuinely useful caveat that survives even though the paper's headline number does not — replicate-derived σ estimates skew HIGH, so the paper's anchors may be upper bounds.

items.headline: Two internal inconsistencies flagged: the repo cites Bruneau for 0.27 in two places, and a separate claimed sentence gives 0.3 as a discard threshold — different quantities, neither verified.
items.verbatim: Also note two internal inconsistencies flagged during verification, which should be resolved before the guide is used: the repository currently cites Bruneau for 0.27 in `REVISION_GUIDE.md` line 357 and `DISCUSSION_TRACKER.md` line 116, while a separate claimed sentence from the same paper gives 0.3 as a *discard threshold* — different quantities that should not be conflated. Neither is verified.
items.why_it_matters: Names the exact two repo lines carrying the unverified number, so they can be struck. NOTE: the DISCUSSION_TRACKER.md:116 reference is to the older layout; the current live warning is at DISCUSSION_TRACKER.md:125.

items.headline: Niu 2024 (PharmaBench) — the verified LogD replacement for Bruneau: repeat-test MAE 0.7 before curation, 0.48 after.
items.verbatim:
> "LogD 0.774 1.196 0.7 0.881 0.881 0.48"

*Location: Table 5, first data row. Caption: "Comparison of Metrics Between the Regression Datasets Before and After the Data Processing Workflow." Column structure: ADMET Property Name | Before Data Processing Workflow (R, RMSE, MAE) | After Data Processing Workflow (R, RMSE, MAE). So LogD before: R = 0.774, RMSE = 1.196, MAE = 0.7; after: R = 0.881, RMSE = 0.881, MAE = 0.48. The repeated 0.881 is genuine, not a transcription error.*
items.verification: verified (open access; Table 5 fetched by direct HTML parse from nature.com)
items.why_it_matters: This is the number that REPLACES the failed Bruneau 0.27. Fully verified, open access, same endpoint, and it sits inside the same 0.4–0.7 band so the conclusion is unchanged.

items.headline: Niu 2024 — the agreement statistics are deliberately worst-case, so any σ derived from them is an upper bound.
items.verbatim:
> "The maximum and minimum experimental results for each group are selected as the worst-case scenario."

*Location: Technical Validation → "Repeated test for data quality assessment", immediately preceding Table 5.*
Establishes that the reported agreement statistics are deliberately worst-case, so any σ derived from them is an upper bound rather than a typical value.
items.why_it_matters: Frames MAE 0.48/0.7 as upper bounds, which is the honest reading and matters for whether σ=0.6 is 'one unit' or 'more than one unit' of real error.

items.headline: Niu 2024 — the standard modern procedure for estimating label noise from a public dataset (repeat records of the same compound).
items.verbatim:
> "A raw dataset often contains multiple records for the same compound due to different sources and varying experimental conditions. Repeated testing compares the maximum and minimum values for the same compound under the same condition to validate the data quality."

*Location: Technical Validation → "Repeated test for data quality assessment".*
Establishes the standard modern procedure for estimating label noise from a public dataset — comparing repeat records of the same compound — which is the empirical basis a noise-injection study should point to when choosing σ.
items.why_it_matters: Gives the paper a documented, current methodology to point at when justifying how a σ can be derived from a public dataset.

items.headline: Niu 2024 — even a well-curated modern LogD benchmark only reaches 'wet-lab-comparable' reproducibility; the noise floor does not vanish with curation.
items.verbatim:
> "The results of repeated tests for certain experiments, such as the LogD experiment, have significantly improved data quality after the data processing workflow, reaching a level comparable to that of traditional wet lab experiments."

*Caveat:* this sentence cites no external wet-lab benchmark; the supporting comparison is the dataset against itself, before versus after processing. The next sentence in the paper explicitly excludes CYP and clearance endpoints from the claim.
items.verification: verified (quote); the caveat notes the comparison is internal, not against an external benchmark
items.why_it_matters: Supports 'the noise floor does not vanish with curation' — the strongest general argument for why label-noise robustness matters at all.

items.headline: Alvarez Baron 2025 — hERG assay repeatability is about five-fold under standardised, ICH-compliant protocols.
items.verbatim:
> "Descriptive statistics and meta-analysis were applied to the dataset to estimate what the distribution in hERG block potencies would be if a laboratory were to test the same drug repeatedly. This measure, or hERG data variability, was ~ 5X."

*Location: abstract. (The space before "5X" is a thin space in the published version.)*
Provides a current, headline-level statement of hERG assay repeatability — about five-fold — that a noise-injection study can quote as the physical meaning of its chosen σ on hERG labels.
items.verification: verified (open access; fetched via Europe PMC PMC12357877 and direct nature.com curl)
items.why_it_matters: The most CURRENT (2025) hERG number, and the one cited in the drafted Methods sentence. 'Even under standardised protocols' is a strong rhetorical position.

items.headline: Alvarez Baron 2025 — the τ figures with an arithmetic caveat: 0.18 alone does NOT generate the 4.9× figure; cite the 0.69 / 4.9× pair.
items.verbatim:
> "The estimated overall variability (τ) not explained by drug and laboratory and expressed as SD was 0.18, and as 95% CI 0.69, corresponding to an IC50 ratio of 4.9X (95% CI: 4.0 to 6.2)."

*Caveat, arithmetic:* 0.18 alone does not generate the 4.9× figure; 0.69 is the half-width of the 95% interval and 10^0.69 ≈ 4.9. If this sentence is used to justify a noise magnitude, cite the 0.69 / 4.9× pair, or the numbers will not reproduce. Also note the paper reports τ as an SD in pIC50 units — pIC50 is already a negative log10, so "log10 pIC50 units" is a unit-of-a-unit error.
items.verification: verified (quote), with an arithmetic caveat that must travel with it
items.why_it_matters: Quoting 0.18 with 4.9× would produce numbers a referee cannot reproduce. The unit-of-a-unit warning is a real trap in log-scale endpoints.

items.headline: Alvarez Baron 2025 — noise magnitude differs nearly three-fold BETWEEN laboratories even under standardised protocols (3.4× to 9.6×).
items.verbatim:
> "The modelling results shown in Fig. 10 also suggest that variability in hERG block potency is laboratory-specific, ranging from 3.4X to 9.6X for different laboratories in this study."

*Location: Discussion, subsection "Limitations and lessons learned" — a verification pass corrected this from the subsection "Variability in hERG block potency". Cite the corrected subsection.*
Establishes that even under standardised protocols the noise magnitude differs nearly three-fold between laboratories, which supports reporting results across a σ range rather than at a single calibrated σ.
items.verification: verified, with a subsection location correction applied by the verification pass
items.why_it_matters: The published argument for reporting a σ RANGE rather than one calibrated point — directly relevant to whether σ=0.6 can stand alone.

items.headline: Alvarez Baron 2025 — the definition of the noise quantity: the distribution of potencies on repeat measurement of the same drug, residual after removing drug and laboratory effects.
items.verbatim:
> "A goal of this study is to assess variability of hERG block potency, which is defined as the distribution of potencies for the same drug when measured repeatedly by the same laboratory."

> "These approaches used strategies to estimate and then remove drug- (i.e., potency) and laboratory-specific impacts (i.e., systematic differences to the group average) to reveal unexplained or residual variability in data not tied to drug or laboratory."

*Location: Results, section "Variability in hERG block potency", third sentence of the opening paragraph (a verification pass corrected this from "second sentence").*
items.verification: verified, with a sentence-position correction applied by the verification pass
items.why_it_matters: Establishes that the reported variability is the irreducible residual — exactly the quantity an injected Gaussian stands in for.

items.headline: Hayeshi 2008 — the four usable abstract quotes (design, mechanism, compound-dependence, qualitative disagreement); NO number is quotable from the paper itself.
items.verbatim:
> "In this study, Caco-2 cells from 10 different laboratories were compared in terms of mRNA expression levels of 72 drug and nutrient transporters, and 17 other target genes, including drug metabolising enzymes, using real-time PCR."

> "Absolute expression of genes was variable indicating that small differences in culture conditions have a significant impact on gene expression, although the overall expression patterns were similar."

> "Atenolol permeability was more variable across laboratories than metoprolol permeability."

> "Talinolol efflux was observed by all the laboratories, whereas only five laboratories observed significant apical uptake of Gly-Sar."
items.verification: verified (abstract only; full text paywalled at Elsevier, abstract fetched via Europe PMC PMID 18782614 and cross-checked via NCBI efetch)
items.why_it_matters: These four sentences are all that can be quoted from Hayeshi. The atenolol/metoprolol contrast is a citable argument for value-proportional or heteroscedastic noise; the Gly-Sar sentence shows disagreement can be qualitative, not just scatter.

items.headline: Hayeshi 2008 gap — no quantitative statement can be quoted from Hayeshi itself; every number attributed to it comes from a secondary source.
items.verbatim: **Hayeshi's own numbers.** No quantitative statement can currently be quoted from Hayeshi et al. 2008 itself, because the full text is paywalled at Elsevier and only the abstract was retrieved. If a number attributed directly to Hayeshi is load-bearing, either obtain the PDF or attribute the number explicitly to Chen et al. 2017 or Kell & Oliver 2015, marked as reported-by.
items.verification: unverified — every Hayeshi NUMBER is secondary
items.why_it_matters: The Caco-2 anchor rests entirely on secondary attribution. Any Hayeshi number in the paper must be marked reported-by or it is a misattribution.

items.headline: Chen 2017 — the quotable Caco-2 magnitude: atenolol efflux ratios ranged 0.18 to 3.76 across 10 laboratories.
items.verbatim:
> "In a collaborative study comparing Caco-2 cells from 10 laboratories, atenolol showed highly variable permeability and its efflux ratios ranged from 0.18 to 3.76, indicating the possibility of an involvement of transporter-mediated transport [38]."

*Location: Discussion, the paragraph on ABC/Pgp transporter evidence, immediately before the sentence beginning "In summary, it is not clear which transporter(s)…". Reference 38 is Hayeshi et al. 2008.*

*Caveat:* this range is Chen et al.'s characterisation of Hayeshi's data, so it should be cited as reported by Chen et al., or checked against Hayeshi directly.
items.verification: verified in Chen et al. (open access, PMC5664587) — but it is a SECONDARY characterisation of Hayeshi's data
items.why_it_matters: This 20.9-fold spread is where the ~0.43 log10 Caco-2 figure in the master table was derived from. Note: memory records that this Caco-2 route is now SUPERSEDED by Bentz 2013's 0.35.

items.headline: Chen 2017 — the Papp range across cell models, with an explicit warning not to re-attribute it to Hayeshi alone.
items.verbatim:
> "The reported Papp values from other in vitro cell models bearing tight junctions for both A–B and B–A directions were in the range of 0.18 × 10−6 − 11 × 10−6 cm/s for Caco-2 cells and 0.13 × 10−6 − 0.8 × 10−6 cm/s for MDCKII (Madin-Darby canine kidney II cells) [37–40]."

*Caveat:* the range is attributed to references [37–40] collectively (Hakkarainen 2010, Hayeshi 2008, Wang 2005, Gartzke 2015). It must **not** be re-attributed to Hayeshi alone.
items.verification: verified (quote); the collective-attribution caveat is explicit
items.why_it_matters: A ~60-fold Caco-2 range that would be very tempting to attribute to Hayeshi. The caveat names all four underlying references.

items.headline: Kell & Oliver 2015 (PeerJ) — the 'factor of 2–5' characterisation of the Hayeshi spread, the only citable magnitude without the paywalled full text.
items.verbatim:
> "An interlaboratory comparison (Hayeshi et al., 2008) indicated that while on occasion measurements could vary by more than an order of magnitude, overall the groupings were normally reasonably tight (say within a factor of 2–5)."

*Location: Kell DB, Oliver SG, PeerJ 2015;3:e1405, Introduction. Retrieved from `https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4655101/fullTextXML`. The dash in "2–5" is an en dash in the original.*

*Caveat:* this is Kell & Oliver's own prose describing Hayeshi, not Hayeshi's text. The factor-of-2–5 figure is verified only as a secondary characterisation and remains unchecked against Hayeshi 2008 itself.
items.verification: verified verbatim in Kell & Oliver — secondary characterisation, unchecked against Hayeshi itself
items.why_it_matters: Factor 2–5 corresponds to 0.30–0.70 log10, which brackets the paper's Caco-2 anchor. Note the same paper is cited elsewhere in the repo as 'O'Hagan & Kell 2015' — same PeerJ 3:e1405.

items.headline: Bentz 2013 — 62% of Caco-2 measurement variance is BETWEEN laboratories; the dominant structure in real error is provenance, not label magnitude.
items.verbatim:
**Bentz J, O'Connor MP, Bednarczyk D, et al. (2013).** *Drug Metab Dispos* 41(7):1347–1366.
23 participating laboratories. Variance decomposition of log efflux ratio (Table 7):

| Source | Share |
|---|---|
| **Laboratory** | **62%** |
| Laboratory × experiment | 20% |
| Residual error | 10% |
| Cell line | 8% |

Also, justifying the modelling scale: *"Log ER and log IC50 were used in variance component
analysis since data are log normally distributed."*

**This is the strongest single argument in the whole design.** The dominant structure in
real label error is *where the measurement came from*, not how big the value was.
items.verification: verified (Table 7 read directly; the log-scale sentence is quoted verbatim)
items.why_it_matters: Called 'the strongest single argument in the whole design'. It is the published basis for the new Grouped (by-laboratory / by-scaffold) noise type and for dropping the four value-dependent ones.

items.headline: Landrum & Riniker 2024 — curating IC50 data to a single assay cuts mean absolute disagreement from 0.50 to 0.27 log units.
items.verbatim:
Corroborating: **Landrum GA, Riniker S (2024)**, *JCIM* 64(5):1560–1567 — curating IC50 data
down to a single assay cuts mean absolute disagreement from **0.50 to 0.27 log units**, so
roughly half the apparent noise in public potency data is provenance, not imprecision.
items.verification: verified (already has a bib entry: citations.bib:1910, key `landrum2024`, and is already cited in paper Methods L211)
items.why_it_matters: Quantifies the provenance share directly — half the apparent noise. This citation is ALREADY in the bib and already used, so it is the cheapest one to lean on.

items.headline: Krüger & Overington 2012 — real bioactivity error is FORMALLY non-Gaussian: Anderson-Darling rejects normality at p<2e-16, and a Laplace fits instead.
items.verbatim:
> "The density distribution of differences in bioactivity has a central peak at 0 and is
> **non-normal as established by Anderson-Darling test (p<2e-16)**."

They then fitted a **Laplace** distribution — *"Both distributions can be approximately
described by a Laplace distribution... the scale parameter b... is b = 0.7 for the paralogs
and b = 1.3 for human-to-rat orthologs."*
items.verification: verified (open access, read in full; 2,782 compound-ortholog pairs, 41,733 paralog combinations)
items.why_it_matters: The only FORMAL statistical test in the whole evidence base that real error is not Gaussian. It is the citational basis for the Student-t and Laplace noise types.

items.headline: Krüger & Overington 2012 — cite it accurately: do NOT inject b=0.7 or 1.3 as measurement error, and do not use words the paper never uses.
items.verbatim:
⚠️ **Cite this accurately.** The paper never uses the words "heavy-tailed", "leptokurtic"
or "Gaussian". Cite what they did — rejected normality, fitted Laplace. Also note their b
values describe differences between *related proteins* (biology); their separate
inter-assay control distribution (measurement error) is stated only to *"closely resemble"*
the ortholog one. **Do not inject b = 0.7 or 1.3 as measurement error.** Take the shape,
dose-match it like everything else.
items.why_it_matters: b=0.7 and b=1.3 look like ready-made noise parameters and are not — they describe biology, not measurement. This warning prevents injecting the wrong quantity.

items.headline: Kramer 2016 (AstraZeneca, every assay 2005–2014) — average experimental uncertainty less than a twofold difference, with no assay type worse than another.
items.verbatim:
- **Kramer C, Dahl G, Tyrchan C, Ulander J (2016).** *Drug Discov Today* 21(8):1213–1221.
  Every AstraZeneca assay 2005–2014: *"an average experimental uncertainty of less than a
  twofold difference and no technologies or assay types had higher variability than
  others."* A constant fold-difference is a constant standard deviation in log space.
items.why_it_matters: Independent industrial corroboration that error is constant in log space — the second of three lines supporting value-independence.

items.headline: Srinivasan & Lloyd 2025 and Horwitz & Albert 2006 — two further lines supporting constant error on the log scale.
items.verbatim:
- **Srinivasan B, Lloyd MD (2025).** *J Med Chem* 68(3):2052–2056. Potency data is
  lognormal; taking logs *"converts multiplicative variability... to arithmetic
  variability"* — constant error on the scale actually modelled.
- **Horwitz W, Albert R (2006).** *J AOAC Int* 89(4):1095. Error scales as concentration to
  the power 0.85 — near-constant *relative* error, i.e. near-constant error in logs.
items.verification: verified (Srinivasan quote); Horwitz power-0.85 stated as a finding, not quoted
items.why_it_matters: Completes the three-way corroboration that a fixed σ in log units is the physically correct instrument — the core of the anchoring argument.

items.headline: Where value-dependence DOES exist it is censoring at the assay limits, not smooth scaling.
items.why_it_matters: Explains why the four value-dependent strategies are replaced by ONE mechanism (censoring) rather than kept — the whole redesign turns on this distinction.

items.headline: Svensson 2025 and the Assay Guidance Manual — censoring is the most PREVALENT real mechanism: 25–63% of labels censored in ten of fifteen industrial assays.
items.verbatim:
**Svensson et al. (2025)** report 25–63% of labels censored in ten of fifteen real
industrial assays, including 8% in a logD assay of 88,114 compounds. Assay Guidance Manual
(NCBI Bookshelf NBK91994): values outside the tested range *"should be '<Xmin' or '>Xmax',
as appropriate."*
items.verification: verified (AGM quote); Svensson percentages stated as reported findings
items.why_it_matters: Censoring turned out to be 12× more damaging than any shape difference in the author's own tests, and this is the published prevalence evidence that it is worth studying.

items.headline: Heid 2023 — noise SHAPE does not matter once the amount is matched; this is already published for homoscedastic noise, so novelty lies in the concentrated case.
items.verbatim:
> "We did not observe any difference in overall model performance between different error
> distributions, **as long as the mean and standard deviation of the noise was the same**,
> respectively. Though noise distributions found in real data may be non-Gaussian, **if
> homoscedastic**, they should still follow the same trends."

This confirms dose-matching is the right move. It also means "shape does not matter at equal
dose" is **already published for evenly-spread noise**. The open question — where novelty
remains — is whether it holds when noise is *concentrated*, either on a structural group
(strategy 4) or on a sparse random subset (strategy 5). Heid explicitly excludes that case.
items.verification: verified (already has a bib entry: citations.bib:683, key `Heid2023`, already cited in Methods)
items.why_it_matters: Simultaneously the published precedent for dose-matching AND the boundary of what is already known — it defines exactly where this paper's novelty sits.

items.headline: Heid 2023 — a misreading this project itself previously made, and the exact sentence to rewrite.
items.verbatim:
⚠️ **Do not claim Heid et al. showed noise is structure-dependent.** A common misreading —
and one this project previously made — is that they *"used mean-variance estimation and
bias-variance decomposition to show that noise can be tied to specific modalities, for
example structure dependence."* They did not. They **imposed**
structure-dependent noise by hand — *"Gaussian noise of standard deviation 20 kcal/mol for
nitrogen-containing molecules and... 2 kcal/mol for non-nitrogen-containing molecules"* —
then showed a method could detect what they themselves injected. Rewrite the sentence.
items.why_it_matters: This misreading is currently IN the paper (RERUN_PLAN.md:777 flags it at paper line :186). It is a live factual error about a cited source.

items.headline: Kolmar & Grulke 2021 — the direct predecessor: they parameterise noise by its standard deviation and report the achieved magnitude in label units.
items.verbatim:
Kolmar & Grulke (*J Cheminform* 2021, **13**:92 — the direct predecessor, same journal, same
experiment) already parameterise noise by its standard deviation: their Eq. 7 is
Y_noise = Y + N(0, σ_noise), with σ_noise set per noise level. They also convert back to label units
when interpreting, writing that for BACE *"1.1 log units of noise were added, or 1.6 times the average
standard deviation reported in ChemBL"*. That is the precedent for both halves of this decision —
parameterising by SD, and reporting the achieved magnitude in units a chemist can read.
items.verification: verified (bib entry exists: citations.bib:39 and scripts/new_citations.bib:140, key `Kolmar2021`)
items.why_it_matters: This is THE precedent for how other noise-injection papers parameterise noise level, in the same journal, on the same experiment. The '1.6 times the average ChEMBL SD' line is the exact move this paper is copying.

items.headline: Kolmar & Grulke — QM9/DFT has no random experimental error, quoted outright.
items.verbatim:
- **QM9 has no assay error to anchor to.** Kolmar & Grulke state it outright: *"quantum
  mechanical calculations do not have random experimental error, because the same
  calculation will give exactly the same number."* For QM9, `k` is the only honest axis and
  the noise is a controlled perturbation, not a simulated measurement.
items.why_it_matters: A published sentence that carries caveat 1 (QM9 exclusion) for free. It means the paper does not have to argue the point itself.

items.headline: Zhao 2017 (ACS Omega) — the published precedent for the k = τ/SD(y) form of noise level.
items.verbatim:
**Precedent for the k form:** Zhao Y, Wang J, Sedykh A, Zhu H (2017). *ACS Omega*
2(6):2805–2812 — *"the standard deviation of each data set was multiplied by a parameter k
(k = 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0)."*
items.why_it_matters: The other convention in the noise-injection literature — noise as a multiple of label SD. This is the citation that licenses the QM9 fraction-of-spread axis.

items.headline: Song 2023 (IEEE TNNLS) — the machine-learning noise-RATE convention does not transfer to regression, and they say so.
items.verbatim:
**Why root-mean-square and not something else:** RMSE and R² are second-moment quantities,
so matching the noise's second moment is what makes them comparable. The machine-learning
convention of fixing the *fraction* of corrupted labels does not transfer — Song et al.
(2023) *IEEE TNNLS* 34(11):8135–8153 define noise by a rate and state explicitly that they
*"focus on the classification setting"*. A flipped class label has no magnitude; a
perturbed continuous label is nothing but magnitude.
items.why_it_matters: Third parameterisation convention in the literature, and the reasoned rejection of it. Pre-empts a referee asking 'why not report a noise rate like the ML literature does?'

items.headline: Hampel 2001 — the source for the outlier contamination fraction p = 1–10%.
items.verbatim:
- **p = 1–10%** — Hampel (2001): *"for scientific routine data, not taken with utmost care,
  their fraction is typically between 1 percent and 10 percent."*
items.why_it_matters: Turns an arbitrary contamination fraction into a cited one. Pairs with Huber 1964 (already in the bib) for the contamination model itself.

items.headline: Four independent lines agreeing on λ = 3, the contamination severity multiplier.
items.verbatim:
- **λ = 3** — four independent lines agree. Solubility within-laboratory error must be
  *"multiplied by a factor of 3"* to reach between-laboratory error (Avdeef 2019,
  *ADMET & DMPK* 7(3):210–219); solubility test sets 0.62/0.17 = 3.6 (Llinàs & Avdeef 2019,
  *JCIM* 59:3036–3040); potency 0.68/0.17–0.22 = 3.1–4.0 (Kalliokoski et al. 2013); and it

items.headline: The hERG stand-in caveat — there is no target-specific published SD for hERG; Kramer's 0.54 is ChEMBL-wide and must be labelled a stand-in.
items.verbatim:
- **hERG has no target-specific published standard deviation.** Kramer's 0.54 is
  ChEMBL-wide and must be labelled a stand-in. It is the right one: the endpoint matches
  (Ki), it is a standard deviation, and it is bracketed by a hERG cross-assay-format RMSD
  of 0.737 (Sato 2018, n=209) and a best-case standardised-protocol residual of 0.18
  (Alvarez Baron 2025).
items.verification: verified reasoning; the 0.54 is explicitly a labelled stand-in
items.why_it_matters: Prevents the paper claiming a hERG-specific published SD that does not exist, while still defending 0.54 as the right stand-in with a bracketing argument.

items.headline: The Caco-2 dynamic-range note and its two corroborating sources.
items.verbatim:
- **Caco-2 is noisier per log unit than it looks**, because its dynamic range is narrower.
  Corroborated by Larregieu & Benet 2013 *AAPS J* 15(2):483–497 (median 0.33, computed) and

items.headline: σ = 0.6 CHOSEN by the author — the decision quote, with the literature block that backs it.
items.verbatim: **✅ D11 → σ = 0.6 CHOSEN (2026-08-20, author: "Why don't we just use 0.6?") — and the literature backs it.** 31-agent verified search (workflow `wf_b419480e-a74`, full output `tasks/wqrlyif68.output`). Published experimental error, in the SAME log units as the labels: hERG pKi **SD 0.54** (Kramer 2012 *JMC* 55:5165); pIC50 **0.68** (Kalliokoski 2013 *PLoS ONE* 8:e61007, 20356 pairs); hERG pIC50 RMSD **0.737** (Sato 2018); logD **MAE 0.48** after curation / 0.7 before, repeat-test worst case (Niu 2024 *Sci Data* 11:985 Table 5, VERIFIED). ⚠ **The Bruneau & McElroy 2006 "0.27" figure FAILED verification — do not use** ... **All estimates fall 0.27–0.74, clustered ~0.5 ⇒ σ=0.6 ≈ ONE UNIT OF REAL EXPERIMENTAL ERROR for every endpoint.**
items.why_it_matters: This is the author's own decision in their own words, with the date and the evidence attached. It is the anchor decision the entire σ discussion converged on.

items.headline: The author's three successive directions on σ, in order, showing how the decision evolved.
items.verbatim:
**D11 → AUTHOR DIRECTION (2026-08-20): "I don't think we need a whole new metric. Just rank R² under a set noise level (we need to determine this level)."** ⇒ no `delivered`/composite metric. Report plain R² read off at ONE σ.
...
**D11 → AUTHOR DIRECTION 2 (2026-08-20): "So it should be a different sigma per dataset" — YES, and it costs NOTHING to run.**
...
**D11 → AUTHOR DIRECTION 3 (2026-08-20): "Every dataset has a different threshold. Determine the threshold on percentage of models falling above/below."** ⇒ drop the label-SD ratio arithmetic; set σ per dataset empirically from where models start failing.
items.why_it_matters: The full decision trajectory in the author's own words. Directions 2 and 3 were both superseded by the literature anchor, but they record what was tried and why it was dropped.

items.headline: auc_norm STAYS — the author's framing that R² at σ=0.6 is a sanity check, not a replacement metric.
items.verbatim: **(a) ANSWERED — `auc_norm` STAYS.** Author's framing: *"auc_norm needs to take into account baseline performance at higher sigmas. The r2 at sigma=0.6 is a bit of a sanity check on auc_norm. Obviously other noise levels exist, but it catches a few cases."* ⇒ NOT a metric replacement; the fix is to make baseline visible beside auc_norm.
items.why_it_matters: Settles whether R²@0.6 replaces auc_norm. It does not — and this quote is what the entire §12 figure spec is built on.

items.headline: The author's approval of the noise-SD dose rule, with the instruction to cite Kolmar in the paper.
items.verbatim: | **The noise level becomes the noise actually delivered** | 2026-08-21 | *"Fine lets do Noise SD, add it to the next steps doc, make sure to cite kolmar and make sure that ends up in the paper (add a note)"* — this is the dose-matching rule. It is approved, and it must appear in the Methods with the Kolmar & Grulke citation |
items.why_it_matters: An explicit, dated author instruction that the Kolmar citation must appear in the Methods. This is a paper-insertion obligation, not a suggestion.

items.headline: THE DERIVATION, part 1 — the discrimination evidence that originally recommended σ=0.8, kept as evidence after being superseded as the method.
items.why_it_matters: The statistical half of the σ argument. It independently rules out σ<0.5 as uninformative, which is what makes 0.6 the lowest defensible choice — the literature and the statistics agree.

items.headline: THE DERIVATION, part 2 — the ranking is locally stable at every σ, so the choice is not knife-edge but it does matter across the range.
items.verbatim: - **Ranking is locally stable**: adjacent-σ Spearman ≥ 0.947 throughout (0.7↔0.8 = 0.982). So no σ choice is knife-edge — but the choice matters across the range (σ=0.2 vs 1.0 = 0.801).
items.why_it_matters: Pre-empts 'why not 0.5 or 0.7?' — the answer is that neighbouring choices give the same ranking, so the literature anchor can carry the decision alone.

items.headline: ARGUMENT AGAINST σ=0.6 — it is NOT where models separate best, and the paper must not pretend otherwise.
items.verbatim:
σ = 0.6 is **not** where models separate best. Model discrimination — between-model spread over
between-fold spread — is flat across the whole grid (1.88 to 2.34, no peak). That is convenient rather
than a problem: 0.6 costs nothing in discriminating power, so the assay-error argument carries it
alone. Do not manufacture a data-driven justification the data does not support.
items.why_it_matters: The honest counter-argument, recorded by the author's own analysis. It explicitly forbids dressing 0.6 up as a data-driven optimum.

items.headline: Two DIFFERENT jobs for σ that must be kept separate in the paper: discriminating between models vs mimicking real noise.
items.verbatim: - **Two DIFFERENT jobs for σ, keep them separate in the paper:** σ chosen to DISCRIMINATE between models (statistical, → 0.8) vs σ chosen to MIMIC REAL EXPERIMENTAL NOISE (physical, → TBD from literature). Either is legitimate; the paper must say which it is doing.
items.why_it_matters: The clearest statement of the conceptual split. Conflating the two is what made the σ discussion go round in circles for days.

items.headline: THE UNITS PROBLEM — one σ is NOT one noise condition; Caco-2 receives ~2.7× the noise-to-signal of LogD at any given σ.
items.verbatim:
| dataset | label SD | σ=0.5 | σ=0.6 | σ=0.8 | σ=1.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| OpenADMET-LogD | 1.191 | 0.42× | 0.50× | 0.67× | 0.84× |
| ChEMBL-hERG-Ki | 0.905 | 0.55× | 0.66× | 0.88× | 1.10× |
| OpenADMET-Caco2_Efflux | 0.434 | 1.15× | 1.38× | **1.84×** | 2.30× |
| QM9 | 1.051 (IQR 1.041–1.065 ⇒ effectively standardised) | 0.48× | 0.57× | 0.76× | 0.95× |

**Consequence for the paper as it stands:** a fixed σ is *not* a fixed noise condition. Caco-2 receives ~2.7× the noise-to-signal of LogD at any given σ. Cross-dataset comparisons at one σ are not like-for-like, and this is the mechanism behind Caco-2 supplying most of the negative-R² cells (it is not purely model fragility).
items.verification: locally re-derived (label SD back-computed as RMSE²/(1−R²) from σ=0 rows; n=1219–1362 per validation dataset)
items.why_it_matters: Surfaced by the author challenging '0.8 seems really extreme'. It affects the paper AS IT STANDS, not just the σ choice — every cross-dataset comparison at fixed σ needs a caveat sentence.

items.headline: An in-house fix for the units problem exists and was NEVER USED — noise_spec.py, with its own docstring condemning the current approach.
items.verbatim: ⚠ In-house fix exists but was **not used**: `KIRBy/src/kirby/noise_spec.py` expresses level as a fraction of label SD and binary-searches the raw σ. Its own docstring: *"This is what makes a level comparable across datasets; the four ad-hoc definitions never were."* The paper run hardcodes raw `SIGMA_LEVELS` (L79).
items.why_it_matters: A working solution already exists in the repo and was bypassed. Its docstring is a self-indictment that a referee could find.

items.headline: The cost of label-SD matching, measured: it equalises the damage but KILLS Caco-2 as a discriminator.
items.verbatim:
- **Matching DOES equalise the damage (validated):** % of baseline R² retained — fixed σ=0.8 gives LogD 90.8 / hERG 65.6 / **Caco-2 53.1**; matched r=0.7 gives 90.8 / 82.1 / **86.1**. ⇒ confirms the fixed-σ Caco-2 collapse was a UNITS artifact, not a dataset property.
- **⚠ THE COST — matching kills Caco-2 as a discriminator.** Model separation (IQR of R² across models): Caco-2 falls 0.200 → **0.057** at r=0.7, and 0.057 ≈ the σ=0 separation (0.068) ⇒ no signal. hERG falls 0.169 → 0.102. LogD unchanged (0.162, since σ=0.8 is its matched level). **Caco-2's apparent discriminating power in current results comes from being hit ~3× harder than the others.**
items.verification: locally computed on the gated set (baseline≥0.3, fold-averaged, 709 configs)
items.why_it_matters: The full argument FOR and AGAINST label-SD matching, with numbers. It also explains a headline result (Caco-2 discriminates best) as an artifact of dose.

items.headline: Caco-2 granularity constraint — its narrow label SD means the 0.1 grid gives only ~4 usable noise levels.
items.verbatim: - **⚠ Caco-2 GRANULARITY:** labelSD 0.434 ⇒ each 0.1 grid step moves r by 0.23. Only ~4 usable levels (0.23/0.46/0.69/0.92) vs 10 for LogD. r=0.7 landing at 0.69 is luck. A calibrated re-run (`noise_spec.calibrate_sigma`) would be needed for finer control.
items.why_it_matters: Explains why the neat r=0.7 match across all four datasets was partly luck, and what a genuine fix would cost.

items.headline: THE THRESHOLD RULE — where each dataset actually breaks, and the finding that LogD reaches no threshold at all.
items.verbatim:
| rule (R²>0.3) | Caco-2 | hERG | LogD |
|---|---|---|---|
| fewer than 75% remain | σ=0.5 (55%) | σ=0.6 (69%) | **never** (88% at σ=1.0) |
| fewer than 50% remain | σ=0.6 (38%) | σ=0.9 (42%) | **never** (88%) |
| fewer than 25% remain | σ=1.0 (23%) | never (41%) | **never** (88%) |

**⚠ LogD reaches no threshold at all** — 88.1% of configs still clear R²=0.3 and 97.7% still clear R²=0 at maximum noise. LogD is insensitive to the entire noise range tested. That is a reportable finding in its own right (and independently matches the earlier "LogD barely discriminates" note), not a defect to hide.
items.verification: locally computed on the gated set
items.why_it_matters: This is the author's third σ-selection method, and it independently lands on σ=0.6 for hERG. The LogD insensitivity is a genuine reportable finding.

items.headline: R²=0.3 is the only workable threshold — R²=0 is never crossed and R²=0.5 is already failed at σ=0.
items.verbatim: **Threshold choice is constrained, not free:** R²=0 is useless (nothing crosses it but Caco-2 at σ=0.9); R²=0.5 is useless the other way (hERG has only 29.6% of configs above 0.5 at σ=0 — already "failed" before any noise). **R²=0.3 is the only workable threshold**, and it coincides with `ROBUSTNESS_BASELINE_THRESHOLD`.
items.why_it_matters: Shows the R²=0.3 gate was not chosen arbitrarily — it is the only threshold the data admits, and it happens to match the existing code constant.

items.headline: OPEN — the threshold percentages POOL the six noise strategies, which violates the no-averaging rule and needs a per-strategy breakout.
items.verbatim: - **⚠ OPEN:** these percentages POOL the 6 strategies (hetero barely degrades, threshold/valprop degrade hard) ⇒ crossing σ will differ by strategy. Needs per-strategy breakout before it goes in the paper, per the no-averaging rule.
items.why_it_matters: An unresolved blocker on using the threshold-rule tables in the paper. It would be silently lost if DISCUSSION_TRACKER.md is deleted.

items.headline: Heteroscedastic noise never separates models at ANY σ — a property of the strategy, not of the cutoff.
items.verbatim: **⚠ Heteroscedastic noise never separates models at any σ** — separation flat at 0.061–0.071 from σ=0 to σ=1.0, median R² only 0.485 → 0.400. Per-strategy separation at σ=0.8: threshold 0.390, valprop 0.219, legacy 0.139, quantile 0.128, outlier 0.122, **hetero 0.063**. This is a property of the strategy, not of the cutoff, and any hetero column in a robustness ranking essentially reproduces the baseline ranking. Needs an explicit caveat sentence wherever hetero is reported.
items.why_it_matters: No σ choice can rescue the heteroscedastic column — it reproduces the baseline ranking in disguise. This requires a footnote on every AUC_norm heatmap.

items.headline: Under mild noise σ=0.6 just reproduces the clean ranking; only threshold and value-proportional noise change who wins.
items.verbatim:
2. **Under mild noise, ranking at σ=0.6 just reproduces the clean ranking** (0.91–1.00 for hetero/legacy/outlier/quantile on LogD and hERG). Noise of this magnitude does not change which model you would pick.
3. **Under the stress strategies it does change** — R²@0.6 vs clean falls to 0.26 (hERG threshold) and 0.20 (hERG valprop), and 0.70 on LogD threshold. **Threshold and value-proportional noise are where robustness actually decides the winner**; the other four largely do not.
items.verification: locally computed from validation_rerun, rep=PDV, gate≥0.3
items.why_it_matters: A direct consequence of choosing σ=0.6: at that level most noise types do not change the answer. This is both a limitation and the strongest support for the three-tier strategy framing.

items.headline: Clean R² and AUC_norm are essentially unrelated — the last column runs −0.36 to +0.49 and sits near zero in 14 of 18 cells.
items.verbatim: 1. **Clean R² and AUC$_\text{norm}$ are essentially unrelated** — the last column runs from −0.36 to +0.49 and sits near zero in 14 of 18 cells. Whatever AUC$_\text{norm}$ ranks models by, it is not how accurate they are. This is the same near-independence seen at model-mean level (Spearman 0.179), now reproduced per dataset × strategy on 13 models.
items.verification: locally computed from validation_rerun, rep=PDV, gate≥0.3
items.why_it_matters: This near-independence is the reason σ=0.6 was needed at all — retention alone does not tell you which model to pick.

items.headline: The clearest demonstration that retention crowns models for having less to lose — on LogD the AUC podium and the accuracy podium share NO models.
items.verbatim:
| Dataset | by R² at σ=0.6 | by clean R² | by AUC$_\text{norm}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| LogD | DNN, GP, MLP | DNN, GP, SVM | **NGBoost, MLP-VBLL-Full, BNN-Full** |
| hERG | RF, LightGBM, QRF | LightGBM, RF, QRF | **NGBoost, RF, SVM** |
| Caco-2 | MLP-VBLL-Full, DNN, MLP | DNN, SVM, GP | **MLP-BNN-Full, MLP-VBLL-Full, GP** |

On LogD the AUC$_\text{norm}$ podium and the accuracy podium share **no models at all**, and the AUC winners are the low-baseline ones — NGBoost's clean R² on PDV/LogD is 0.661 against DNN's 0.797. This is the clearest single demonstration that the retention metric crowns models for having less to lose.
items.verification: locally computed from validation_rerun (13 models, 48,510 rows), rep=PDV, gate≥0.3
items.why_it_matters: The single most persuasive figure-worthy result from the σ=0.6 work, and the direct justification for the §12 figure changes.

items.headline: The revised per-dataset noise grids, each anchored in log units to one unit of that endpoint's real assay error — this SUPERSEDES the old eleven-point σ ladder.
items.verbatim:
| Dataset | One unit of real error | Proposed levels (log units) |
|---|---|---|
| logD | 0.15 within a lab; 0.50 between methods | 0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0 |
| Caco-2 | 0.35 between 11 labs | 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.7 |
| hERG | 0.54 (stand-in) | 0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.54, 0.8, 1.1 |

Each grid brackets one unit of real error and runs to roughly twice it. Report the resulting
fraction-of-spread alongside, because **one unit of real error is 0.13 of the label spread on
logD but 0.76 on Caco-2** — a factor of six. A single shared ladder would mean six different
experiments.
items.verification: n-a (design decision, sourced to the §4 anchor table)
items.why_it_matters: This is where all the literature work actually LANDS — the per-dataset grids. Each level is now a published assay-error figure, not a round number.

items.headline: QM9 gets a fraction-of-spread axis, set by the range-finding run, because no assay error exists to anchor to.
items.verbatim:
**QM9 — no assay error exists**, so fraction-of-label-spread is the only honest axis.
**Grid set by the range-finding run (§5.5): 0, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5.** Below 0.2 the
models are indistinguishable from clean; 1.5 is retained because it is the only level where
the noise types separate at all.

**Censoring is swept separately** on its own axis — fraction of labels clipped — because it
has no variance parameter and is not zero-mean. **Grid set by the range-finding run (§5.5): 0, 10, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50%.** There is no sharp
knee — damage accelerates smoothly, becoming serious around 20% and severe past 30%.
items.verification: n-a (design decision; grids set by the range-finding run)
items.why_it_matters: Implements caveat 1 (QM9 exclusion) concretely. The two axes are now different quantities and the paper must present them separately.

items.headline: σ=0.6 survives the translation to the new design — on the experimental datasets it becomes 0.6 log units, still one unit of published assay error.
items.verbatim:
**This supersedes the old eleven-point ladder.** Your choice of 0.6 as the reporting level
survives the translation intact: on the experimental datasets it becomes 0.6 log units, which is
still one unit of published assay error, and it is still a sanity check on the retention metric
rather than a replacement for it.
items.why_it_matters: Confirms the σ=0.6 decision is NOT invalidated by the noise redesign. Everything in this salvage remains live.

items.headline: The two-axis reporting rule that resolves the whole σ argument: τ in label units for choosing/realism, k = τ/SD(y) for reporting/comparison.
items.verbatim:
| Axis | Use it for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **τ in the label's own units** (log units for the experimental sets) | **Choosing** the noise levels, and claiming realism | Assay error in log units is roughly constant across endpoints *regardless of label spread*, so a fixed value in log units is more defensible as "one unit of real error" than a spread-matched one |
| **k = τ / SD(y)** | **Reporting** and cross-dataset comparison | Unitless, so electronvolts and log units land on one axis, and it is what determines how hard the learning problem becomes |

**Report both.** They are not interchangeable: a dataset with a narrow label spread suffers
far more from the same absolute error, which is exactly why Caco-2 degrades first
(τ ≈ 0.35 log₁₀ but a narrow dynamic range).
items.why_it_matters: This is the synthesis that ends the fixed-σ vs SD-matched argument: both, for different jobs. It is the durable form of everything above it.

items.headline: The dose-matching rule — each strategy solves for its own scale so the delivered noise amount is equal, and the current six strategies are one strategy at six doses.
items.verbatim:
**Control the realised dose τ: the root-mean-square noise actually added, in the label's
own units.** Every strategy must deliver the same τ, or a comparison between strategies is
measuring amount rather than shape.

This is the fix. Today a single knob is set and each strategy delivers whatever it happens
to deliver — between 0.49× and 2.00× the Gaussian amount on QM9. **τ must be the result,
not the knob.**
items.verification: measured on QM9 (first 10,000 molecules, gap in eV)
items.why_it_matters: The confound that invalidated the entire six-strategy comparison, stated in one paragraph. The 0.49×–2.00× spread is the measured evidence.

| Threshold | 2.000 |
| Value-proportional | 1.701 |
| Gaussian | 1.000 |
| Quantile | 0.899 |

items.headline: Once σ IS the achieved noise SD, the σ=0.6 anchor gets stronger — it becomes literally true for every strategy, not just Gaussian.
items.verbatim:
3. **The σ = 0.6 anchor survives and gets stronger.** Published assay error is 0.54 log units for hERG
   pKi, 0.27–0.62 for logD and about 0.43 for Caco-2 (Kalliokoski et al., *PLoS ONE* 2013, **8**:e61007
   reports σ_pIC50 = 0.68). Once σ *is* the achieved noise SD, "σ = 0.6 is one unit of assay error"
   becomes literally true for every strategy rather than true only for Gaussian.
items.verification: the logD 0.27 lower bound in this sentence is the FAILED Bruneau figure and must be corrected to 0.48 (Niu 2024); the Caco-2 0.43 is the SUPERSEDED Hayeshi/Chen route and should be 0.35 (Bentz 2013)
items.why_it_matters: The dose-matching decision and the literature anchor reinforce each other. But this sentence carries two stale numbers that must be updated before use.

items.headline: Do not truncate the σ grid — only half the damage has happened by σ=0.6, and a second reporting point at σ=0.9 is recommended.
items.verbatim:
- **Do not truncate the grid.** Only about half the total damage has happened by σ = 0.6 and the
  curves are still steep above it. Report a second point at σ = 0.9 where robustness rather than
  baseline skill dominates the ordering.
- **Report damage per dataset, not pooled.** Mean relative drop at σ = 0.6 differs 3.4-fold: LogD
  0.155, hERG 0.356, Caco-2 0.529.
- **σ = 0 stays permanently** as a negative control.
- **Do not rescale the grid by each dataset's label standard deviation.** Assay error is absolute in
  log units and roughly constant across these three assays, so an absolute scale is the physically
  correct instrument.
items.why_it_matters: Four settled sub-decisions about the grid, including a concrete recommendation (a second point at σ=0.9) that is not recorded anywhere else.

items.headline: The three-number reporting rule, with Kolmar & Grulke as the precedent for printing all three in the same cell.
items.verbatim:
- **Clean R² (σ = 0)** — can this model and representation learn the property at all. Precondition for
  the other two meaning anything.
- **R² at σ = 0.6** — what you actually get when labels carry roughly one unit of real assay error.
- **`auc_norm`** — the shape of the decline, each model divided by its own clean score so models with
  different starting accuracy can be compared on decline alone.

in the same journal for the same kind of ratio); and make the existing 0.3 clean-R² gate visible in the
printed tables, so a reader can tell a real 0.97 from a meaningless one.

items.headline: THE §12 FIGURE SPEC — the decision in the author's framing, and the five concrete changes it implies.
items.verbatim:
**The decision, in the author's framing:** AUC$_\text{norm}$ **stays** as the robustness metric. It is not replaced. The problem is narrower than "wrong metric" — AUC$_\text{norm}$ needs to carry baseline performance alongside it, because on its own it rewards a model for having had little to lose. **R² at $\sigma = 0.6$ is a sanity check on AUC$_\text{norm}$, not a competing metric.** Other noise levels exist; this one catches a useful set of cases.

That framing is what these changes implement. Nothing here proposes a new metric or a new figure.

items.headline: §12.4 — the new third panel on fig3 (R²@0.6 vs AUC_norm) and the three worked cases that land in the flattered quadrant.

items.headline: Threshold noise is an accident of a unit conversion — its cut catches 99.9992% of QM9 molecules and would have caught zero in Hartree.
items.verbatim:
`threshold` has a second, independent problem: its cut fires on `|y| ≥ 1.0` against raw
electronvolts, and QM9's smallest gap is 0.67 eV, so **99.9992% of molecules clear it**.
It is homoscedastic Gaussian noise at double dose, with no threshold behaviour at all. Had
the pipeline stayed in Hartree the same cut would have caught *zero* molecules. Its entire
character is an accident of a unit conversion.
